titleStmt.title: A Dependency-Graph Based Priority Assignment Algorithm for Real-Time Traffic over NoCs with Shared Virtual-Channels

analytic.title: A Dependency-Graph Based Priority Assignment Algorithm for Real-Time Traffic over NoCs with Shared Virtual-Channels

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Network-on-Chip (NoC) is the on-chip interconnection medium of choice for modern massively parallel processors and System-on-Chip (SoC) in general. Fixed-priority based preemptive scheduling using virtual-channels is a solution to support real-time communications in on-chip networks. Targeting the priority assignment problem in the context of NoCs, heuristic based priority assignment algorithms are more practical, due to the exponentially increased search space as the number of flows goes up. In our previous work, we have proposed a graph-based heuristic priority assignment algorithm (called GHSA) for NoC communications, where we show that taking the dependencies between flows into account can significantly reduce the search space. However, GHSA only works for NoCs with distinct priorities. Routers in such type of platforms may have a large amount of buffer cost when the number of flows is high. The applicability can thus be limited in reality. One solution to reduce the buffer cost is to allow priority sharing of different flows. In this paper, we propose a dependency-graph based priority assignment algorithm (called eGHSA) targeting NoCs with shared virtual-channels. A number of experiments as well as a case study based on an automotive application are generated, which clearly show that eGHSA improves the efficiency compared to the existing solution in the literature.
1 A flow refers to a series of packets with the same given characteristics.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The Network-on-Chip (NoC) has been proposed as a preferred interconnection medium for massively parallel platforms as well as for System-on-Chip (SoC). Compared to the traditional bus-based interconnection mediums, the NoC is more scalable for a large number of elements. It connects multiple Intellectual Property (IP) cores, where each IP core can provide different functionalities, even possibly from different vendors. In order to function correctly, the IP cores may need to exchange data frequently through the NoC. Thus the NoC is crucial in order to guarantee correct functionalities of each IP core and the system in general. Additionally, timeliness of communications over NoCs becomes more and more important if such platforms are intended for real-time applications. For such applications, each packet needs to be delivered within a certain deadline.
In this paper, we focus on NoCs using a fixed priority based scheduling which is favored for many real-time applications.

One of the most important issues for fixed priority scheduling is the priority assignment which has been well studied in the context of processors. Even though a NoC channel has similar characteristics as a single-core processor, the complete network cannot directly be related to the results from scheduling theory of processors. In specific, as discussed in [1], Audsley's optimal priority assignment algorithm [2] is not optimal for NoCs.

In [1], the authors have proposed a heuristic priority assignment algorithm (called HSA) targeting wormhole-switched NoCs with distinct priorities (i.e. each flow 1 has a unique priority which uses one isolated Virtual-Channel (VC) [3]). Unfortunately, using distinct priorities can lead to a significant buffer cost, since each VC requires a specific buffer on each router. Such a design may not be practical for many industrial applications since the hardware cost should be seriously considered. Therefore, in [4], a priority sharing policy (i.e. multiple flows sharing the same VC) is proposed where an extension of HSA is also presented (called eHSA hereinafter). Given a flow set with initial distinct priorities, eHSA can find the lowest number of required VCs. However, the processing time of eHSA increases dramatically as the number of flows goes up, because eHSA is based on an exhaustive search (i.e. it examines the whole search space). Such a limitation makes eHSA less applicable in practice. For example, during the design phase of a real-time system, a designer may need to iteratively generate task mappings until a valid mapping is found. For each mapping, a priority assignment process needs to be applied to find a valid schedule. In this case, an inefficient priority assignment process can slowdown the whole design phase. Therefore, in this work, we aim to provide a more efficient priority assignment algorithm for NoCs with shared priorities. Note that eHSA is already based on an exhaustive search given a set of flows with distinct priorities, thus the number of required VCs cannot be improved further.

In our previous work [5], we have proposed an undirectgraph based priority assignment algorithm (called GHSA) for NoCs with distinct priorities. The evaluation results clearly show that taking the dependencies between flows into account can reduce the search space of the algorithm. The efficiency of the assignment process can thus be improved. In this paper, we investigate how to use the assistance from dependency-graphs of flows to achieve a more efficient priority assignment in the context of wormhole-switched NoCs with shared priorities.

div.head: A. Contribution
div.p: In this paper, we present the following contributions: 1) We present a dependency-graph based priority assignment algorithm (called eGHSA) for NoCs with shared virtual-channels. Compared to the state-of-the-art solution presented in [4] (called eHSA hereinafter), the proposed eGHSA can achieve the same number of utilized VCs but requiring less computation time. 2) We revise the existing schedulability test [6] for NoCs with a priority sharing policy in order to reduce pessimism. 3) A number of experiments are generated along with a case study based on an automotive application, in order to evaluate the proposed algorithm. The results are represented by the number of required schedulability tests as well as the actual processing time from the measurements, where the improvement can be clearly observed.

div.head: B. Related Work
div.p: The NoC is implemented as interconnection medium on several massively parallel processors in order to cope with the increased data volume [7][8] [9]. As many platforms target the embedded industry, an increased interest lies on the real-time requirements for traffic on NoCs [10] [11].

Wormhole switching/routing is not a new technology [12]. Recently it has become more and more popular for onchip networks due to its low buffer requirements and high scalability. Wormhole switched networks with virtual-channels are first presented by Dally in [3]. Later Song et al. examined such networks and their applicability for real-time traffic by introducing preemption to the fixed-priority flows [13].

Priority assignment for single processor systems is a widely studied problem. In [14], Liu and Layland presented the Rate Monotonic (RM) priority assignment, and Leung and Whitehead later presented the Deadline Monotonic (DM) priority assignment to fit more general task models [15]. Audsley's optimal priority assignment algorithm [2], [16] guarantees to find a priority assignment in a polynomial number of schedulability tests, if one exists.

In the context of fixed-priority preemptive NoC, Mutka was the first to develop priority assignment algorithms [17]. The major work on priority assignment for fixed-priority preemptive NoC was done by Shi and Burns in [1]. They present a branch and bound based heuristic algorithm (HSA) to assign priorities to NoC flows with distinct priorities.

The Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) arbitration for wormhole switched NoC has been proposed in [18]. When flows traverse single hops, EDF is optimal as for single processor scheduling and dominates the other approaches. Similar to fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, the single processor results do not hold anymore when longer flow paths are considered. In their experiments, it is shown that for flows with multi-hop paths, HSA assignment by [1] always performs better. The drawback of the above works is the assumption that an exclusive priority (as well as an exclusive VC), is required for each flow. This means that the number of required VCs is equal to the total number of priority levels. [19] shows that this assumption does not hold, and they present an algorithm to reduce the number of needed virtual channels without affecting the schedulability of the systems. Shi and Burns also extend their work [1] to support NoCs with a limited number of VCs by using a priority sharing policy [4]. An extended version of HSA (called eHSA hereinafter) is also proposed in [4] targeting NoCs with shared priorities. However, eHSA does not take the relations between flows into account. For example, while assigning a flow to a certain priority level, the algorithm performs schedualbility tests on all the flows which can potentially be affected. However, for many of these checked flows, their transmissions actually do not affect the flow under assignment at all. Therefore, rechecking the schedulability of such flows is an unnecessary operation which obviously degrades the efficiency of the priority assignment process. In this work, we use the assistance of dependencygraphs of flows to eliminate unnecessary operations involved in a priority assignment process.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: A number of NoC designs have been proposed regarding different requirements. In this paper we focus on wormhole switched NoCs with virtual-channels. In wormhole switched networks, a packet is divided into so called flits. A flit represents the data size which can be transmitted between two routers during one cycle. When a router receives a flit of a certain packet, it can starts to transmit the received flit without waiting for the arrival of the complete packet. Each packet has a header flit which contains most of the routing information such as the path, the flit count, etc. A VC [3] (see Fig. 1) is an additional buffer connected to the physical channel, which can achieve separation between flows sharing the same physical channel. Each VC is bound with a specific priority level. When a flow using the VC with a higher priority arrives at a certain router, it can preempt the transmission of other flows using VCs with lower priorities (i.e. preemptions can happen between different priority levels / VCs). This way each physical channel can be shared by multiple VCs. Each VC can also be shared by multiple flows. The flows sharing the same VC are transmitted using a FIFO (First-In-First-Out) mechanism (i.e. no preemption allowed between them).

The network uses a 2-dimensional mesh-based topology, which is commonly used for many existing implementations (e.g. [8][9]). Each pair of adjacent nodes are connected by full-duplex links. The network contains a set of n periodic or sporadic real-time flows
div.formula: F = { f 1 , f 2 ,... f n } (n ∈ N + ). Each flow f i can be characterized by (C i , T i , D i , R i ). C i represents
div.p: the basic transmission latency of f i which is the transmission time without any blocking or interference. T i denotes the minimum inter-arrival time between two successive instances for sporadic flows, or the period for periodic flows. D i is the relative deadline of f i . A flow is schedulable only if its transmission can meet the deadline (i.e. the response time is no larger than the relative deadline). In this paper, we assume that all the flows have constrained deadlines (i.e. D i ≤ T i ) 2 . Each flow has a fixed transmission route which is denoted as R i .

div.head: III. PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT OF NOC FLOWS WITH PRIORITY SHARING
div.p: In this section, we present eGHSA, which aims to assign priorities to flows in a NoC with a priority sharing policy. First, we revisit and revise the schedulability test for NoC communications presented in [4] [6], and a less pessimistic RTA is proposed. Then we present the details of eGHSA, where the proposed analysis is utilized.

div.head: A. Improved Schedulability Test
div.p: In [4], the authors propose the first Response Time Analysis (RTA) of flows over a wormhole-switched NoC with a priority sharing policy. However, the authors in [6] have discussed that the analysis presented in [4] can result in optimistic results, and a revised RTA is thus proposed. First, we recapitulate this revised RTA. Then we identify the source of pessimism which will be improved later.

As discussed in [6], the response time of a NoC flow f i is mainly affected by four factors: direct interference from higher priority flows; indirect interference through higher priority flows which can cause direct interference to f i ; direct and indirect blocking from flows sharing the same virtual-channel.

A flow f n which shares the same VC with f i can block the transmission of f i . Direct and indirect blocking can both completely affect the response time of f i , therefore they are considered in the same manner during the analysis [6]. Given any time duration Δt, the blocking delay that f n can cause to f i can be upper bounded by Δt T n •C n . We use S(i) to represent all the flows which can cause direct or indirect blocking to f i .

A flow f j , which has higher priority than f i and shares at least one physical link with f i , can preempt and delay the transmission of f i . This type of interference that f j causes to f i is called direct interference. However, if a flow f p has a higher priority than f j but does not share any link with f i , f p can still affects the response time of f i by reducing the minimum inter-arrival times of successive instances of f j . This type of interference that f p causes to f i is called indirect interference.

Under the priority sharing policy, if a flow f n ( f n ∈ S(i)) gets interference from a higher priority flow f j ( f j ∈ S D n ), the whole virtual-channel will be preempted by f j . As a result, f i which shares the same virtual-channel with f n may completely suffer from the interference caused by f j , even if f i does not share any link with f j .

div.head: B. The eGHSA
div.p: In this section, we present a dependency-graph based heuristic priority assignment algorithm (called eGHSA) for NoCs with a priority sharing policy. The time analysis presented in the previous subsection is used to check the schedulability during the priority assignment process. Note that the following priority assignment algorithm does not rely on any specific timing analysis (i.e. using other analyses do not affect the priority assignment process). Targeting the same priority assignment problem, the authors in [4] have presented a heuristic algorithm (i.e. eHSA). Similar to the observation discussed in [5], eHSA does not take the relations between flows into account. As a result, eHSA may involve a number of unnecessary operations which can actually be skipped. However, these unnecessary operations can be avoided by using a dependency-graph as shown in our proposed eGHSA.

eGHSA is presented in Alg. 1. The algorithm mainly involves two phases: (1) assigning a distinct priority to each flow; (2) shrinking the priority levels by merging multiple flows into the same priority level.

We first create a dependency-graph of the whole flow set F . A dependency-graph consists of a number of vertices which are connected by undirected edges (e.g. Fig. 4). Each vertex represents a NoC flow, and the edges show the relations between different flows. Each pair of connected flows share at least one physical link in the network. Fig. 4 shows the dependency-graph of the flow set presented in Fig. 2. The proposed priority assignment algorithm is based on such constructed dependency-graphs. Then we use GHSA [5] 5 to find a valid priority assignment for all the flows in F (line 2). If GHSA fails, the flow set is determined to be unschedulable (line 3-5), and the algorithm terminates directly. Otherwise, GHSA finds a unique priority of each flow in F , where all the flows can meet their deadlines.

The assigned priority of each flow is called its initial priority. The next step is to merge multiple priority levels (i.e. try to assign multiple flows to the same priority level). The newly assigned priority of each flow after the merging process is called its global priority, which is the final priority of each flow. Note that each flow only maintains one priority which will be used in the response-time analysis during the priority assignment. In other words, once a flow receives its global priority, its initial priority becomes obsolete. All the flows are marked as unassigned in the beginning. Once a flow receives its global priority, it is marked as assigned.

algorithm starts from the lowest priority level, and tries to assign all the unassigned flows to the current priority level if possible (line 9-37). The checking process starts from the flow which has the lowest priority among the remained unassigned flows (i.e. f i in line 13). While trying to assign f i to the current priority level P c , the algorithm needs to check the schedulability of the assigned flows since their response times may get affected [4] (line 17-26). Only if all the assigned flows as well as f i can meet their deadlines, f i is assigned to P c and marked as assigned (line 30). This implies that all the assigned flows must be schedulable. Otherwise, f i is still marked as unassigned and will be checked later for higher priority levels (line 27-28).

However, during the assignment of f i to P c , some of the flows may not be affected, whose schedulability tests can thus be skipped. Definition 1. In a dependency-graph, f i and f j are considered to be actively disconnected in any of the following cases: A. f i and f j are not connected at all (e.g. Fig. 5-a end if 37: end for 38: return Schedulable with N R VC Fig. 5-b); C.
f i and f j are connected, but the connection must pass through a third flow f k which has a lower priority than f i and f j (e.g. Fig. 5-c).
Theorem 2. While assigning f i to the current priority level P c , if f i and an assigned flow f j are actively disconnected, the schedulability of f j will not be affected.
Proof. Based on the three cases presented in Definition 1, the proof is divided into three cases as well.

For Case A in Definition 1: If f i and f j are not connected at all, they must belong to two separate dependency-graphs. In this case, their transmissions cannot affect each other at all, since neither blocking nor interference can occur between them.

For Case B in Definition 1: In this case, f i and f j are not directly connected, which means that they do not share any physical links. Therefore, f i can cause neither direct interference nor direct blocking to f j . The intervening flow f k is unassigned, which implies that f k has a higher priority than f i and f j . If f i can cause indirect blocking to f j , f i and f j as well as all the intervening flows in between must have the same priority according to the definition [6]. However, this contradicts to the condition that the intervening flow f k has a higher priority. Therefore, f i cannot cause indirect blocking to f j .

On the other hand, since f k has a higher priority than f i , assigning f i to P c (i.e. P c is no higher than the initial priority of f i ) will not increase the response time of f k . The interference jitter of f k will thus not be increased. Consequently, f j will not experience an increased interference from f k .

Therefore, assigning f i to P c will not increase the response time of f j , so the schedulability of f j will not be changed. For Case C in Definition 1: Similar to Case B, f i cannot cause any direct interference or direct blocking to f j , since they do not share any link.

A contradiction to the condition that the intervening flow f k has a lower priority than f j can be observed, if f i causes indirect blocking to f j . Therefore, f i cannot cause indirect blocking to f j either.

According to the definition of indirect interference, if f i can cause indirect interference to f j , f i must have a priority higher than the intervening flow f k , and f k has a priority higher than f j . However, this contradicts to the condition that f k has a lower priority than f i and f j . Consequently, f i cannot cause any indirect interference to f j .

Therefore, assigning f i to P c will not affect the response time of f j at all. According to Theorem 2, if f i and f j are actively disconnected, we can directly skip the schedulability test of f j (line [18][19]. The algorithm repeats the above assignment process until all the flows have received its global priority. The algorithm then returns the number of required virtual-channels (line 38). In the worst-case, eGHSA returns N R VC = n, which means that no flows can share the same priority level.

For some cases, system designers may want to verify if a given set of flows can be schedulable on a specific hardware implementation. In other words, the number of VCs is fixed and known in advance. In this case, we can still use eGHSA with a slight modification. While shrinking the priority levels (line 9-37), we can monitor the change of the required virtual-channels. Once the number of required virtualchannels becomes smaller than or equal to the given number of virtual-channels, the algorithm can be terminated since the requirement is already fulfilled. In this case, the network fully utilizes all the given virtual-channels instead of compressing the required virtual-channels as much as possible. As we can observe from the analysis presented in Section III-A, a flow can only get an increased or equal WCRT when it shares a virtual-channel with other flows compared to the case when it monopolizes the virtual-channel. Therefore, fully utilizing the given virtual-channels can decrease the average response times of the flow set compared to the setting with fully shrunk priority levels, while still keeping the time requirement satisfied.

div.head: IV. EVALUATION
div.p: As discussed in Section III, our proposed eGHSA aims to improve the efficiency of priority assignment by using dependency-graphs to reduce the number of required schedulability tests. Therefore, the evaluation presented in this section focuses on the efficiency of eGHSA compared to eHSA [4]. In order to achieve a fair comparison, the timing analysis presented in Section III-A is used for both eGHSA and eHSA. Note that in the experiments, the schedulability ratio and the number of required VCs achieved by eGHSA and eHSA 6 are both examined as well. However, the results show that eGHSA and eHSA always give the same performance with respect to schedulability ratios and number of required VCs. Therefore, in the following sections, we only show the results regarding the efficiency which is the main difference between eGHSA and eHSA.

div.head: A. Case Study
div.p: First, we evaluate the proposed algorithm using a case study. The case study is based on an autonomous vehicle application, which has been used in [22] [23]. In this application, the system contains a number of tasks performing different functionalities such as obstacle detection through stereo photogrammetry, navigation control, and stability control. There are 38 real-time flows transmitted in the network for inter-task communication. The application is deployed on a 4 × 4 2D meshed NoC platform which uses the XY routing algorithm. More details of the flow set can be found in [22].

In [22], the authors have shown that the flow set is schedulable with distinct priorities. After applying eGHSA and eHSA, we notice that the flow set is actually schedulable using only one priority level with the task mapping given in [22]. Fig. 6 shows the comparison between eGHSA and eHSA regarding the number of required schedulability tests. Mapping 1 refers to the task mapping utilized in [22], and the other five task mappings are randomly generated to show the variation 7 . As shown in the results, eHSA requires the same number of schedulability tests no matter how flows are allocated, since it does not take the relations between flows into account. On the other hand, the proposed eGHSA always requires a significantly lower number of schedulability tests. As the allocation of flows changes, the number of required schedulability tests changes accordingly.

div.head: B. General Evaluation
div.p: In addition to the case study, we also generate a number of general evaluations. The following experiments use a network based on a 8 × 8 2D-mesh based topology. The flows are transmitted using the XY-routing mechanism, where the sources and destinations are randomly generated. The number of flows is generated from (10,20,30), and the average traffic utilization per link is controlled within the range of [0.2, 1]. The basic transmission time of each flow is randomly generated from the range of [1,1000] time units with a granularity of 1. The utilization of each flow is randomly generated using the UUnifast-Discard algorithm [24]. Given the basic transmission time C i and the utilization U i of each flow, the period is computed as C i /U i . We divide the experiments into five groups which have different numbers of flows in the network varying from 25 to 125. The results of each group are obtained from 1000 samples 8 .

First, we present the results regarding the number of schedulability tests involved in the priority assignment algorithms. As shown in Fig. 7, when the number of flows in the network goes up, the complexity of eGHSA and eHSA increases, which results in more required schedulability tests. However, eGHSA always requires a lower number of schedulability tests compared to eHSA. This shows that, with the help from the dependency-graph, a significant number of unnecessary schedulability tests can be avoided.

Using a graph-based search algorithm can indeed reduce the search space for HSA and eHSA, but processing the dependency-graphs actually causes additional overhead. Therefore, we need to measure if the benefit gained from the graph-based search algorithm can compensate the extra overhead. We measure the processing time of the experiment sets presented above in true time.

As discussed earlier, eGHSA and eHSA both rely on assigned distinct priorities. The main difference occurs during the priority shrinking process. Therefore, we first show the comparison between eGHSA and eHSA regarding the priority shrinking process. The results are illustrated in Fig. 8-a, and the details are listed in Table I. According to the results, when the number of flows is low (e.g. 25 and 50), the processing times of eGHSA and eHSA are quite close. The average processing time of eGHSA is shorter than eHSA, but the maximum processing time of eHSA is lower than eGHSA. This shows that when the number of flows in the network is low, the overhead caused by the graph-based search algorithm may overshadow its benefit for some cases. However, as the total number of flows goes up, the benefit from the graph-based search algorithm becomes more and more obvious. When the number of flows is 100, the average processing time of eHSA is 9.7%9 longer than eGHSA, and the maximum processing time of eHSA is 36.5% larger than eGHSA. Additionally, we also implement measurements on the processing time of a complete priority assignment procedure. In these experiments, we compare the solution using our graphbased search algorithm (i.e. GHSA [5] with eGHSA) and the existing priority assignment approach without assistance from dependency-graphs (i.e. HSA [1] with eHSA [4]). The results are presented in Fig. 8-b and Table II. As shown in the results, compared to the existing approach, using the proposed graph-based search algorithm can always achieve a shorter average processing time. As the number of flows increases, GHSA+eGHSA precedes HSA+eHSA more and more. When the number of flows is 125, the average and maximum processing times of HSA+eHSA are 12%10 and 25% longer than GHSA+eGHSA respectively. Moreover, by comparing Table I and Table II, we can also observe that the distinct priority assignment process (i.e. GHSA or HSA) is faster than the priority shrinking process (i.e. eGHSA or eHSA).

According to the above measurements, we can conclude that the graph-based search algorithm can indeed reduce the search space of priority assignments. An additional overhead is incurred as a price due to traversing the constructed dependency- graphs. However, compared to the existing approach, the improvement in efficiency using the proposed algorithms can still be clearly observed, especially when the network has a larger number of flows. Moreover, priority assignment algorithms can also be used in some task mapping solutions (e.g. [25]). After generating each candidate mapping, a priority assignment algorithm is applied to check the schedulability of the flow set. Since a complete task mapping process may involve a large number of candidates, the priority assignment process is thus repeated for many times. For these applications, the improvement in the efficiency of the proposed algorithm becomes even more significant.

V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK In this paper, we present a dependency-graph based priority assignment algorithm targeting NoCs with shared priorities/virtual-channels. In the proposed algorithm, dependencies between flows are taken into account in order to avoid unnecessary schedulability tests. The efficiency of the priority assignment process can thus be improved. A number of experiments have been generated along with a case study, in order to evaluate the proposed algorithm compared to the existing approach. The results clearly show that while achieving the same number of required virtual-channels, eGHSA is more efficient, especially when the network contains a large number of flows.

Looking at the future work, we would like to combine the priority assignment problem together with the task mapping problem. In this paper, we assume that the sending and receiving tasks of each flow are already allocated on specific cores before applying the priority assignment process. However, the allocations of flow routes can actually affect the schedulability of the whole flow set. By considering both problems together, better solutions may be derived which can achieve higher schedulability ratios compared to the existing works.
